 Takeaways from Maryland men’s basketball’s 86-74 crosstown loss to Georgetown
 The Terps struggled from beyond the arc on offense and defense.
 by Dylan Schmidt Nov 8, 2026, 11:40 AM UTC Facebook 
 Link 
 Maryland men’s basketball head coach Buzz Williams took ownership for the team’s slow start against Bucknell earlier this season. But in Saturday’s game against Georgetown, the issue only furthered.
 The Terps opened a 9-7 lead just over four minutes into the contest, but they trailed for the remainder of the game. Maryland faced a 12-point deficit on the heels of a 22-8 Hoyas’ run, and the damage only got worse — Georgetown created an 80-53 lead with five minutes remaining.
 Despite closing the game on a 10-0 run, the Terps were outmatched, falling 86-74 in their first hurdle of the season.
 Here are three takeaways from the loss.
 3-point disparity continues 
 Maryland was not shy about shooting from deep early on — it fired nine 3-point attempts in the first 11 minutes. But the success was nonexistent.
 Andre Mills connected on a shot from deep at the 16:48 mark. The redshirt sophomore, who went 34.4% from 3-point range last season, contributed the Terps’ only make in the first half. While Maryland continued to hoist looks from behind the arc, none found nylon.
 Seven different players attempted a 3-point field goal in the first half, but the shots didn’t fall. Even Mike McNair Jr. — the nation’s fifth-best shooter from behind the arc last season — missed his lone first-half look.
 After Mills nailed the 3-point attempt, Maryland missed the next 17 shots from deep. While Kaden House snapped the drought with four minutes remaining after a pair of makes, the damage was already done.
 That 27-point deficit largely came from Georgetown’s perimeter success.
 The Hoyas were hot early, raining in five of their first 10 3-point shots. Guards Elmarko Jackson and Jaland Lowe were the primary beneficiaries. The duo each totaled 14 first-half points, with Lowe hitting four of his six 3-pointers. Jackson nailed a pair of first-half shots from deep, helping account for Georgetown’s eight first-half triples.
 Maryland — which allowed Bucknell to splash 12 3-pointers Monday — was hit with a barrage of shots from behind the arc. After a 7-for-26 showing in the season opener, Georgetown finished with a 50% 3-point percentage and 15 makes.
 Meanwhile, the Terps hit just three of 20 attempts from deep, their lowest percentage in the last three seasons.
 Pharrell Payne runs the show 
 While Mills was the primary aggressor early — he had five of the first nine points and fired four quick shots — Payne’s presence in the paint helped alleviate the lack of perimeter success.
 Battling against a pair of Georgetown 7-footers, Payne imposed his will on the glass. The redshirt senior corralled four offensive rebounds in the first half, translating to his scoring production. Payne had a team-high 10 first-half points on 5-for-7 shooting.
 Despite his size disadvantage, the 6-foot-9 stretch center bullied his way through the crowded paint for shot attempts right at the rim — his five first-half makes all came via layups.
 Payne came out of halftime with an urgency, looking to fuel the Terps back from a 16-point halftime deficit. He got to the free-throw line on Maryland’s first offensive possession after the break, and drew five fouls in the second half.
 While Payne converted eight free throws in his final 13 minutes on the court, he remained a steady presence inside. Payne poured in a game-high 18 second-half points and only missed four shots in the game, largely due to his work on the offensive glass — seven of his eight rebounds helped create second-chance opportunities for Maryland.
 “That’s one of our team pillars is rebounding,” Payne said. “I feel like we take a lot of pride in going to the offensive glass as well as trying to keep a high percentage of defensive rebounds.”
 Foul trouble proved costly 
 Even with Georgetown posting 44 points in the first half, the Terps weren’t whistled often. Mills and Bishop Boswell were Maryland’s only players with two fouls at halftime.
 But that completely changed in the second half.
 The Terps committed four fouls on Georgetown’s opening possession, with McNair called for three of them. The graduate student, who was scoreless in his 22 minutes, helped the Hoyas quickly get in the bonus.
 While Georgetown continued its relentless shooting in the second half, it also got to the free-throw line at a high clip. The Hoyas attempted 19 free throws, but only made 57.9% of those shots. Still, the significance was larger than that.
 Payne and McNair each finished with four fouls, forcing Williams to continue to roll with four-guard lineups. Georgetown capitalized, hauling in six offensive rebounds in the second half that led to 11 points.
